1.title: Selecting Claude Models
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Selecting Claude Models. This module covers selecting claude models. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. The Claude model tiers and what each is for. The trade-offs: capability, latency, cost, context, availability. Effort, thinking and fast mode as tuning levers. Routing and cascades across tiers. How to justify a choice with evals and pin it for production.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Picks Models for a Bank's Three Workloads
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Picks Models for a Bank's Three Workloads. Intent classification of two million messages a day, answers needed in under a second. Drafting replies from policy, moderate volume, quality matters. Quarterly regulatory analysis across hundreds of pages, run overnight, correctness-critical.

1.title: The Tiers and the Levers
1.text: The Tiers and the Levers. Fable five point one. Positioning: Demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. Latency: Slower. Price per MTok in or out: ten dollars or fifty dollars. Default effort: high. Opus five point five. Positioning: Long-running agentic coding and knowledge work; start here for most workloads. Latency: Moderate. Price per MTok in or out: four dollars or twenty dollars. Default effort: medium. Sonnet five point five. Positioning: Best combination of speed and intelligence. Latency: Fast. Price per MTok in or out: two dollars or ten dollars. Default effort: high. Haiku five point five. Positioning: High-volume, latency-sensitive tasks: classification, extraction, routing. Latency: Fastest. Price per MTok in or out: from zero dollars and ten cents or zero dollars and fifty cents. Default effort: medium.

1.title: The Tiers and the Levers, continued
1.text: The Tiers and the Levers, continued. The figure shows this: Model tiers trade speed and price for capability: Haiku is fastest and cheapest, Sonnet balances, Opus is stronger, Fable is the most capable and slowest. All current models: one million token context window, text and image input, one hundred twenty-eight thousand max output (synchronous), reliable knowledge cutoff June two thousand twenty-six.

1.title: The Tiers and the Levers, continued
1.text: The Tiers and the Levers, continued. Pricing levers: Batch A P I (application programming interface) fifty percent off; cache reads cost ten percent of base input (five percent on Opus five point five and Sonnet five point five, two point five percent on Fable five point one); cache writes one point two five times (five-minute) or two times (one-hour). Effort (low to max) is a behavioral signal that trades thoroughness for tokens, latency and cost; adaptive thinking lets the model decide how much to think. Fast mode buys higher output speed at premium pricing on supported models. Model I Ds are pinned snapshots: pin the full I D in production, test before moving, and plan for retirement dates (Anthropic-operated platforms: not sooner than two thousand twenty-seven).

1.title: The Tiers and the Levers, continued
1.text: The Tiers and the Levers, continued. Platforms: Claude A P I, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry, Claude Platform on A W S. Availability, regional endpoints and compliance differ by platform (Module fourteen). Exam tip: Questions give a binding constraint (latency, cost, quality, compliance) and ask for the tier or lever. Name the tier by the role (classification equals light, general equals balanced, hard reasoning equals strong).

1.title: Making the Choice
1.text: Making the Choice. The figure shows this: Model selection flow: define the quality bar with evals, start with a balanced tier, step down when a cheaper tier passes, step up only when evals fail, then pin the model I D.

1.title: Making the Choice, continued
1.text: Making the Choice, continued. High-volume classification, extraction, routing. Likely choice: Haiku (low effort). Why: Latency and cost dominate; the task is bounded. Customer-facing drafting, summarization. Likely choice: Sonnet. Why: Quality and speed balanced. Complex analysis, agentic coding, long documents. Likely choice: Opus. Why: Reasoning depth pays off. Hardest problems where evals on Opus at high effort still fail. Likely choice: Fable. Why: Highest capability; accept latency and cost. Non-urgent bulk jobs. Likely choice: Any tier through Batch. Why: fifty percent saving when latency does not matter. Evals decide. Choose the smallest model that passes your eval; "always the largest" and "always the smallest" are both wrong.

1.title: Making the Choice, continued
1.text: Making the Choice, continued. Routing: a cheap classifier (or Haiku) sends easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a larger model. Cascade: try the cheap model first and escalate on low confidence or failed validation. Tune before upgrading: better prompt, retrieval or examples, then effort, then model tier. Retest on every model change: behavior and prompts can shift; run regression evals. Match context needs: a one million window does not replace retrieval for very large corpora (Module nine).

1.title: Trade-Off Table
1.text: Trade-Off Table. Lower latency. Pull this lever: Smaller tier, lower effort, streaming, caching, shorter output. Cost of the lever: Possible quality loss. Lower cost. Pull this lever: Smaller tier, caching, batch, shorter prompts, routing. Cost of the lever: Latency (batch) or quality. Higher quality. Pull this lever: Stronger tier, higher effort, thinking, better retrieval. Cost of the lever: Cost and latency. Compliance. Pull this lever: Platform and region choice, Z D R or B A A eligible features. Cost of the lever: Feature availability, setup. Stability. Pull this lever: Pinned snapshot, regression evals. Cost of the lever: Delayed access to improvements. Exam tip: The smallest model that passes the eval wins; "always the largest" and "always the smallest" are both distractors. Exam tip: Tune in order: prompt and retrieval, then effort, then tier; pin the model I D and retest on every change.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Tiers: Haiku fastest or cheapest, Sonnet balanced, Opus strong, start here for most, Fable strongest, slowest. Common: one million context; one hundred twenty-eight thousand output; cutoff June two thousand twenty-six. Savings: Batch fifty percent off; cache reads ten percent (five percent or two point five percent on some tiers). Rule: Smallest model that passes the eval. Patterns: Route by difficulty; cascade on low confidence. Tune order: Prompt and retrieval, then effort, then tier. Pin: Full snapshot I D; regression evals on change.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A bank classifies two million messages per day into twelve intents with a sub-second target. Which choice fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Bounded, high-volume, latency-sensitive classification is the light tier's role.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. An overnight regulatory analysis is correctness-critical and latency does not matter. Which combination is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Quality-first model with batch discounts suits non-urgent, critical work.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A team wants to save cost without hurting quality. What is the best method? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Evals prove the cheaper tier is good enough.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Why should a production system pin the full model I D? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Pinning gives stability; move only after regression evals.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A router sends easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a large model. Which benefit does this give? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Routing aligns capability and cost with task difficulty, so average cost and latency fall while hard cases still get the stronger model.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two levers reduce latency for an interactive assistant? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Streaming improves perceived latency; smaller tier and lower effort cut generation time.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Evals on the balanced tier fail on the hardest ten percent of cases even after prompt and retrieval improvements. What is the next step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Step up only on evidence, ideally for just the hard slice.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: D. Question two: B. Question three: A. Question four: D. Question five: D. Question six: B and E. Question seven: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
